answer_text:
Let

\[
x=2^m \qquad (x>1).
\]

Then

\[
4^m-1=x^2-1=(x-1)(x+1).
\]

Since

\[
\gcd(x-1,x+1)=\gcd(x-1,2)=1,
\]

any divisor of \((x-1)(x+1)\) can be written as a product of a divisor of \(x-1\) and a divisor of \(x+1\). Thus there exist positive integers \(a,b\) such that

\[
n=ab,\qquad a\mid x-1,\qquad b\mid x+1.
\]

The condition \(2^m\mid n-1\) means

\[
x\mid n-1,
\]

so for some integer \(q\ge 1\),

\[
n=ab=1+qx.
\]

Also, since \(b\mid x+1\), write

\[
x+1=bt
\]

for some positive integer \(t\). Then \(x=bt-1\), so

\[
ab=1+q(bt-1)=1+qbt-q.
\]

Hence

\[
ab-qbt=1-q,
\]

or

\[
b(qt-a)=q-1.
\]

Therefore

\[
b\mid q-1. \tag{1}
\]

On the other hand, since \(a\mid x-1\), we have \(a\le x-1\). Thus

\[
q=\frac{ab-1}{x}\le \frac{b(x-1)-1}{x}
= b-\frac{b+1}{x}<b.
\]

So

\[
q<b. \tag{2}
\]

If \(b=1\), then \(a=n=1+qx\ge x+1\), which is impossible because \(a\mid x-1\) forces \(a\le x-1\). Hence \(b\ge 2\).

From \(q\ge 1\) and \(q<b\), we get

\[
0\le q-1<b.
\]

But by (1), \(b\mid q-1\). The only possibility is

\[
q-1=0,
\]

so \(q=1\). Therefore

\[
n=1+x=1+2^m.
\]

Thus it is indeed forced that

\[
\boxed{\text{Yes, necessarily } n=2^m+1}.
\]
